title: Mock contest: search, sets, number reasoning, greedy, partition DP
overview: A practice contest before the final. The first three problems need simple tools: a linear search, a `set` for unique sorted letters, and a little number reasoning. The last two files hold only the problem statements, so the notes explain how to attack them: a sort-then-greedy idea and a subset DP with a size limit.

concepts.explain: Scan from the left and return the first index where the value matches; return -1 if you reach the end.
Keeps unique elements in sorted order automatically, so inserting every character and then printing the set gives unique letters alphabetically.
3, 4, 6, 7, 8 are reachable, and since 6, 7, 8 are three consecutive values, adding 3 again covers every number from 6 upward. Only 1, 2 and 5 are impossible.

concepts.term: Sort, then greedy with a falling cap
concepts.explain: To take distinct counts from bags, sort sizes from large to small and take `min(size, previous - 1)`, never below 0.

concepts.term: Balanced partition with a size rule
concepts.explain: Choose exactly n/2 items whose sum is as close as possible to half the total. A DP over (items used, sum) records which sums are reachable.

files.title: The Lost Book (linear search)
files.what: Returns the 0-based index of the target code in the array, or -1 if it is missing.
steps: Read `n`, the array, and `target`.
`lostBook` loops `i` from 0 to n-1 and returns `i` at the first match.
If the loop ends, return -1.
Print the result.
files.input_note: n, the book codes, then the target. This is the contest's first sample.
files.output_note: Prints `4`, because code 3 is at index 4 (counting from 0).
files.watch_out: The array is not sorted, so binary search would be wrong here.

check.q: What would the program print for target 99 with the same array?

files.title: Letters in Order (set of characters)
files.what: Puts every character into a `set<char>`, which removes duplicates and sorts them, then prints the set.
steps: Read the string `S`.
Insert each character into `unique_letters`.
Loop over the set and print each character (already in alphabetical order).
files.input_note: One lowercase string. This is the contest's second sample.
files.output_note: Prints `abn`: the letters b, a, n without repeats, in alphabetical order.

check.q: How could you do this without a set?
check.a: Use a `bool seen[26]` array, mark each letter, then print the marked letters from a to z.

files.title: Guess the No (sums of 3 and 4)
files.what: Decides whether T can be written as a sum of 3s and 4s. It lists the small reachable values and says YES for everything from 12 up.
steps: Anything else (only 5 is left): NO.
files.input_note: A single T. 5 is the interesting case: 3 + something never makes 5.
files.output_note: Prints `NO`. With T = 10 it prints YES (3 + 3 + 4).
files.watch_out: The long condition works, but the rule is simply: NO for 1, 2 and 5, YES for everything else.

files.title: Here Comes the Genie (statement only)
files.what: Take balls from bags so that the counts taken from different colours are all different (zeros may repeat), maximising the total. The file contains only the problem statement.
steps: Sort the bag sizes from largest to smallest.
Take all balls from the largest bag: `cap = a[0]`.
For every next bag take `cap = min(a[i], cap - 1)`; once `cap` reaches 0, take 0 from the rest.
Add up the amounts in a `long long`.
Why it works: the biggest bags should get the biggest distinct counts, and each count should be as large as allowed.
files.complexity: Time O(n log n) · Space O(1) extra
files.input_note: The file has no code, so nothing runs.
files.output_note: No output. With the plan above, the samples work out: [1, 4, 5] -> 5 + 4 + 1 = 10, and [1, 1, 2, 1] -> 2 + 1 + 0 + 0 = 3.
files.watch_out: Only the statement was saved; there is no solution in this file. Use `long long` for the total (up to 2x10^5 values of 10^9).

files.title: Mina and Moni (statement only)
files.what: Split n coins into two groups of sizes n/2 and n - n/2 so the difference of their sums is as small as possible. The file contains only the problem statement.
steps: Let `total` be the sum and `k = n / 2` the size of the smaller group.
Build `can[c][s]`: can exactly `c` coins sum to `s`? Start with `can[0][0] = true`.
For each coin, go through `c` from high to low and mark `can[c+1][s + coin]` from `can[c][s]` (0-1 knapsack style).
For every `s` with `can[k][s]`, the difference is `abs(total - 2*s)`; print the smallest.
Use a bitset per count if the sums are large.
files.complexity: Time O(n·k·total) (faster with bitsets) · Space O(k·total)
files.input_note: The file has no code, so nothing runs.
files.output_note: No output. For coins 1 2 3 10 the best split is {1, 10} vs {2, 3}, difference 11 - 5 = 6, matching the sample.
files.watch_out: Only the statement was saved; there is no solution in this file. Plain subset sum is not enough: the group sizes are fixed, so the DP must also track how many coins are used.

check.q: Why must the DP track the number of coins, not only the sum?
check.a: Each sister must get exactly n/2 (or n/2 + 1) coins; a subset with the right sum but the wrong size is not allowed.

files.title: Minimum Deletions to Make Character Frequencies Unique (LeetCode 1647)

problem.name: Minimum Deletions to Make Character Frequencies Unique

files.what: Counts every letter, then deletes as few characters as possible so that no two letters are left with the same count. Same greedy shape as "Here Comes the Genie" above: sort the counts from big to small and let each one fall to the first free value.
steps: Count the letters in `int freq[26]`. Only 26 letters exist, so no map is needed.
Copy the counts that are above 0 into a vector; a letter that never appeared cannot clash with anything.
Sort that vector from big to small with `greater<int>()`.
Walk it with a cap called `allowed`. The first count keeps everything, so `allowed` starts at the largest count.
For each count, `keep = min(count, allowed)`, and `count - keep` characters are deleted.
Then `allowed = keep - 1`, clamped at 0, because the value `keep` is now taken and the next letter must land lower.
Zero is the floor on purpose: any number of letters may be deleted away completely and all sit at 0 together.
files.input_note: One lowercase string. Counts are a 3, b 3, c 2 - the smallest case where two letters really do clash.
files.output_note: Prints `2`. The first 3 stays, the second 3 falls to 2 (one deletion), and c must then fall from 2 to 1 (one more), leaving counts 3, 2, 1. For `ceabaacb` the program also prints 2.
files.watch_out: Do not stop the cap at 1. Letters are allowed to vanish, so the cap must be able to reach 0, otherwise a string like `aaabbbccc` is counted wrong.

check.q: The string `bbcebab` has counts b 4, c 1, e 1, a 1. How many deletions?
check.a: 2. Sorted 4, 1, 1, 1: the 4 stays, the first 1 stays, the next 1 falls to 0, and the last 1 falls to 0 as well.

files.title: Partition Array Into Two Arrays to Minimize Sum Difference (LeetCode 2035)

problem.name: Partition Array Into Two Arrays to Minimize Sum Difference

files.what: Splits 2n numbers into two groups of exactly n and returns the smallest possible difference of the two sums. This is "Mina and Moni" with the hard version of the rules: the numbers may be negative, so the sum cannot be used as an array index, and the answer is found by meet-in-the-middle instead.
steps: Cut the array in half: the first n numbers and the last n numbers.

Loop over all 2^n bit masks once. For each mask read off the sum it takes from the first half and the sum the same mask takes from the second half, and file both under `taken` = how many bits are set.
So `left[c]` holds every sum reachable by taking exactly c numbers from the first half, and `right[c]` the same for the second half.
Sort each `right[c]`, because the search below needs it in order.
The finished group takes k numbers from the first half and n - k from the second. Loop k from 0 to n.

If the group sums to S, the other side sums to `total - S`, so the difference is `|total - 2*S|`. With `sumLeft` fixed, the aim is a partner p whose `2*p` lands as close as possible to `target = total - 2*sumLeft`.
Binary-search `right[n-k]` for the first p with `2*p >= target`, then compare that p and the one just before it - the best partner is always one of those two.
Keep the smallest difference seen over every k and every subset.
files.complexity: Time O(2^n · n + 2^n · log(2^n)) for n up to 15, about a million steps · Space O(2^n)
files.input_note: First the count of numbers (always even, here 4 so n = 2), then the numbers. This is the problem's own first sample.
files.output_note: Prints `2`: {3, 9} sums to 12 and {7, 3} sums to 10. Run with `6` and `2 -1 0 4 -2 -9` it prints `0`, because {0, -1, -2} and {2, 4, -9} both sum to -3. With 30 random values of size up to 10^7 it still answers instantly.
files.watch_out: The Mina and Moni DP over (count, sum) does not work here, because the numbers can be negative and a sum cannot index an array. Also keep the `2 *` inside the binary search comparison rather than halving the target - halving an odd number would round and pick the wrong neighbour. Sums are held in `long long`; 15 values of 10^7 doubled is still safe in `int`, but `long long` costs nothing and removes the worry.

check.q: Why group the subsets by how many numbers they take, instead of just listing all 2^n sums?
check.a: Because the two groups must have exactly n numbers each. A subset with a perfect sum but the wrong size is not a legal half, so the count has to be carried alongside the sum.

recap: Unsorted data: linear search; do not binary search.
`set` gives unique + sorted in one step.
For 'sums of a and b' problems, find the small impossible values; beyond them everything works.
Sort descending and use a falling cap to make counts distinct.
Fixed group sizes turn subset sum into a DP over (count, sum).

check_yourself.q: Which values cannot be made from 5s and 3s?
check_yourself.a: 1, 2, 4 and 7. From 8 on everything works (8, 9, 10 are reachable and adding 3 covers the rest).

check_yourself.q: What is the running time of inserting m characters into a `set<char>`?
check_yourself.a: O(m log k), where k (at most 26) is the number of distinct letters, so effectively O(m).

body: A contest is not really a test of how much you know. Two hours, five problems, one screen: what decides the day is how fast you turn a story into the right tool, and how rarely you have to throw code away and start again.

So do not start with the story. Start with the constraints line. Those two or three dull lines tell you how much work your solution is allowed to do. A judge gives you about one second, and one second is roughly 100 million simple steps. Read the largest `n` and turn it into a budget:
intro.trace:
n up to        what fits in ~1 second
-------------  --------------------------
20             2^n, try every subset
5 000          n^2, two nested loops
2 x 10^5       n log n, sort / set / map
10^6           n, a single pass
10^9           a formula, O(1) per query

body: Here is why that table is worth thirty seconds. Suppose `n` can be 2 x 10^5 and your first idea is the honest one: for every element, look at every other element. That is 4 x 10^10 steps, and it will score zero. The constraints told you so before you typed a character.
The same table works the other way round. If `n` is only 20, stop looking for something clever: trying all 1,048,576 subsets is fine. A small limit is a hint, not an accident.
With the budget known, read the question again and look for its **shape**. Most beginner-contest problems are one of a handful of sentences in disguise:
intro.trace:
"is x in this list?"
   unsorted -> one scan;  sorted -> binary search
"which values appear, and how often?"
   -> frequency array, map or set
"sum of positions L..R, asked many times"
   -> prefix sums
"take as much as possible, all different"
   -> sort, then a greedy scan
"pick some items to reach a total"
   -> DP over (items used, sum)

body: The pattern this contest leans on hardest is the fourth one: **sort, then be greedy with a falling cap**. It is worth doing once by hand.

Four crates hold 5, 5, 3 and 2 apples. You may take a different number from each crate (taking 0 from several crates is allowed) and you want as many apples as you can. Sort the crates biggest first and keep a `cap`, the largest count you are still allowed to take. Empty the first crate, then drop the cap by one each time and take `min(crate, cap)`:
intro.trace:
crate    5    5    3    2   (sorted, biggest first)
cap      -    4    3    2
take     5    4    3    2

total = 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 = 14

body: Two sentences say why that cannot be beaten. The biggest crates should carry the biggest counts, because a small crate cannot use a big count anyway. And once the cap is fixed, taking less than `min(crate, cap)` from a crate never lets a later crate take more, since the cap only falls. Note also that the cap must never go below 0 - you cannot take -1 apples.

**A second angle: count by hand before you loop.** Questions of the form "can this total be built from 3s and 4s?" look like they need a search. Write the first twelve answers on paper instead. You will usually find a short list of impossible values and then "yes from here on", and the whole problem collapses into an `if`.

**A third angle: read what the question fixes.** If it fixes the total you are aiming at, plain subset sum is enough. If it also fixes *how many* items you may pick, the table needs a second index for the count - same idea, one dimension more.

Three habits save more marks than any algorithm. Check the sample by hand before submitting. Ask whether any total can pass 2 x 10^9 and reach for `long long` if it can. And check whether the answer wants a 0-based or a 1-based index, which is the cheapest wrong answer there is.

The five entries below take the contest's problems one at a time: two short ones you should finish in minutes, one that is pure number reasoning, and two where only the statement was saved, so the notes describe the plan instead of the code.
